title: We shipped a mobile game as a two-person indie studio using Claude as our dev backbone, here's the workflow that actually worked (and what broke everything)
author: B01t4t4
selftext:
Hey fellows,

Two of us — a product manager and a 3D/2D artist — just shipped our first game 

as CariocaRealm, our indie studio. This post is about the AI-assisted dev workflow 

that made it possible for someone without a full engineering background to ship 

a production Android game.

The game is Super Heart Attack — a hypercasual dodge & collect for Android.

But this post is really about the workflow.

\---

🧠 THE CORE INSIGHT THAT CHANGED EVERYTHING: SPECS AS CONTRACTS

Early on I tried the obvious approach: describe a feature in chat,

get code, paste it in, fix what broke, repeat.

It worked for small things. It fell apart completely for anything involving

multiple files, Phaser scene events, or shared state.

The shift that fixed it: I stopped asking Claude to write code directly

and started asking it to write a SPEC FIRST.

A spec file (kept in \`.planning/phases/\`) that contained:

\- ASCII layout of the component

\- Per-element behavior descriptions

\- Constants block (exact variable names, Phaser event names, asset paths)

\- Explicit restrictions ("do not touch Food.js in this pass")

\- Grep-based acceptance criteria ("verify that HUD.js contains \`scene.events.on('combo-update')\`")



Then I'd hand THAT file to Claude Code (the CLI agent) as the grounding contract.

The result: the agent stopped hallucinating variable names,

stopped touching files it shouldn't, and produced code that actually fit

the existing architecture.

\---



🛠️ THE STACK

\- Phaser.js — game engine (scene-event architecture)

\- Capacitor — Android packaging (web → native, no React Native)

\- Firebase — Auth, Firestore (global leaderboard), Analytics, Remote Config

\- AdMob — monetization via u/capacitor-community/admob

\- Vite — build tool

\---

🤖 HOW WE SPLIT THE AI WORK

My partner (3D/2D artist) handled all original art and animations —

sprites, effects, visual identity. No AI art generation there, all original work.

On the dev and product side:

\*\*Claude (Sonnet mostly but I've also used for coding Gemini Flash on Antigravity IDE):\*\*

\- Architecture decisions and tradeoffs

\- Spec writing — turning vague feature ideas into structured markdown 

  that an agent could execute

\- Code generation via Claude Code (CLI) against the spec

\- Debugging sessions with relevant file context



\*\*Gemini:\*\*

\- Visual concepts and layout mockups used as reference for my partner

\- Asset direction iteration (fast to generate, used as mood boards)



Knowing which tool to reach for saved a lot of wasted context.

Claude reasons better about architecture and code contracts.

Gemini is faster for visual iteration.

\---

⚠️ WHAT BROKE (AND WHY)

1. \*\*Images as the only spec source\*\*

   Pasting a screenshot and saying "make it look like this" produced code

   that looked right but had wrong event names, wrong asset paths,

   and silently broke other scenes. The image told Claude \*what\*,

   but not \*how it fits into the existing codebase\*.

   Fix: annotated images as layout REFERENCE ONLY, spec file as the contract.



2. \*\*Context window drift on long sessions\*\*

   On complex features, early instructions got ignored by the \~15th message.

   Fix: restart sessions with a fresh context injection from the spec file

   rather than continuing a degraded thread.



3. \*\*AdMob vs AdSense confusion\*\*

   Asked Claude about monetization setup without being specific —

   got mixed answers because it conflated the two products.

   Fix: always name the exact SDK (\`@capacitor-community/admob\`)

   in every monetization question.

\---

🎮 THE GAME

Super Heart Attack — dodge junk food, collect healthy food, survive,

climb the global leaderboard. Free on Android. First release from CariocaRealm.

👉 [https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.superheartattack.app](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.superheartattack.app)



First week: 10+ downloads, 0 reviews. The grind is real 😅

  


\---

Happy to go deeper on any part of this — the spec workflow,

Phaser + Capacitor integration, Firebase leaderboard, or Play Store publishing.



What's your current AI-assisted workflow? 

Curious whether others have solved the "agent touches the wrong files" problem differently.

comments.body: I think Claude threw up all over your post

replies.author: B01t4t4
replies.body: Bom, não completamente. Eu tive auxilio para organizar o texto, mas a partir de um rascunho que fiz no Obsidian e as proprias documentações que criei para auxiliar o processo de implementação.

comments.author: DaedalusRaistlin
comments.body:
I'm a little perplexed by your flow.

I typically use VS Code with Claude. I' use the chat mainly, and will start each new feature by getting it to plan it out. Sometimes it's a big feature, sometimes it's not. I ask it to grill me on everything so it has all the context I thought was fairly clear. And I check the plan and make sure it fits. Then I just tell Claude to start implementing the first phase. Check what's done before committing and moving onto the next phase. 

Claude generally is using a test skill - it knows how to run a headless browser, and can check that what it's doing works. This is important, it catches visual bugs as well as code bugs. 

This has been working pretty well for me for a few months now. I generally use Opus, on Extra High thinking. Though the two days I got to use Fable were pretty nice - it seemed to be able to play the games and verify their behaviour better than Opus. 

I do use Sonnet and even Haiku for smaller things - updates to small command line tools, or writing a script for mass update of JSON data. Even use ones like Raptor for this occasionally too. 

Google's Gemini I've become less of a fan of. I think it's alright for initial prototypes and a few revisions, but it doesn't handle large codebases well in my experience. 

Also, I don't understand teams who are fine with AI coding but draw the line at AI art. My prompts for artwork are so large I wrote my own image generation suite using Gemini/NanoBanana to overcome the character limits on most services. It's still just a tool. I could take offence that you don't have 30 years of programming knowledge like I do, and are using AI to do that part. But I care more about the final product than how it was made. 

But I think it's cool to see more people getting into coding, even with AI help. I *wish* I had this stuff back when I was learning. Having nobody to ask because it was 1998 and the internet was barely a thing in Australia. I wrote the worst code trying to learn. But I read so many examples and demo's that I eventually got the hang of it. 

Even people like you who are fine with using AI for code still have to clarify your artwork isn't AI. It just boggles my mind really. The thing I spent 30 years learning is fine for an AI to take over, but heaven forbid I use it to help me do the art side I've always struggled with. Then people usually tell me either I pay someone, or use Ms paint. Because apparently if I can't afford to pay an artist, I'm not allowed to have appealing graphics. 

Like your AI code argument, let the results speak for themselves. If my artwork looks crap that's on me and my process breaking down, not the fact I used AI. Or I could argue the same thing about code.

replies.author: B01t4t4
replies.body:
eu não tive boa experiência ao fazer o Claude rodar bem usando o browser para testar a gameplay do jogo. Daí eu deleguei isso pro Gemini. No Antigravity IDE com o browser integrado, ele foi muito assertivo. 

Definitivamente eu não usei o Opus, pois eu tenho apenas o PRO disponível, e é um modelo muito caro. Então a estratégia era mastigar um pouco as tarefas para o Sonnet não se perder. Na maior parte do tempo tive sucesso com isso.

Outro ponto interessante foi quando era necessário fazer qualquer coisas que envolva o Firebase, o Gemini era muito melhor sem muita explicação. O que me surpreendeu positivamente. 

Obrigado pelo seu comentário.
